'''Adam Ezra Cohen''' (born 1979) is a Professor of Chemistry, Chemical Biology, and Physics at [[Harvard University]]. 
He has received a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]]<ref name="whitehouse1">{{Cite web |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/administration/eop/ostp/pressroom/11052010 |title=President Honors Outstanding Early-Career Scientists |access-date=2011-05-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170128053633/https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/administration/eop/ostp/pressroom/11052010 |archive-date=2017-01-28 |via=[[NARA|National Archives]] |work=[[Office of Science and Technology Policy]] |url-status=live }}</ref> and been selected by [[MIT]] ''[[Technology Review]] ''to the [[TR35]] list of the world's top innovators under 35.<ref name="auto">{{cite news|url=http://www.technologyreview.com/TR35/Profile.aspx?TRID=608|title=2007 YOUNG INNOVATORS UNDER 35, Adam Cohen, 28. Harvard University, Making molecules motionless|date=October 3, 2009|work=Technology Review|publisher=MIT|access-date=May 3, 2011|archive-date=April 16, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110416115853/https://www.technologyreview.com/TR35/Profile.aspx?TRID=608|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Early life and education==

Cohen was born in 1979 in New York City, New York. He is the son of [[Joel E. Cohen]], Abby Rockefeller Mauze Professor of Populations at [[Rockefeller University]] in New York. He attended [[Hunter College Elementary School]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/03/11/nyregion/electrochemical-paintbrush-wins-westinghouse-science-competition.html|title='Electrochemical Paintbrush' Wins Westinghouse Science Competition|first=Jacques|last=Steinberg|newspaper=The New York Times|date=11 March 1997|publisher=|access-date=14 February 2017|archive-date=24 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181024192215/https://www.nytimes.com/1997/03/11/nyregion/electrochemical-paintbrush-wins-westinghouse-science-competition.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and [[Hunter College High School]], a magnet school in [[New York City]].<ref name="electrochemical1">{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/invent/iow/cohen.htm|title=Lemelson-MIT Program|website=web.mit.edu}}{{dead link|date=June 2020|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> He graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] and summa cum laude from [[Harvard College]] with an A.B. in chemistry and physics. He received a Ph.D. in  [[theoretical physics]] from [[Cambridge University]], where he was a [[Marshall Scholar]], in 2003,<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/Issues/2008/February/Careers.asp |title=Careers: Young inventor |date=February 2008 |work=Chemistry World |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry |access-date=May 3, 2011 |archive-date=October 21, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021054704/http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/Issues/2008/February/Careers.asp |url-status=live }}</ref> and a Ph.D. in [[experimental physics]] from Stanford in 2006 with [[W.E. Moerner]]. 
Cohen completed a postdoctoral fellowship in chemistry at [[Stanford University]] in 2007.

==Career==
===Research===

Cohen's research combines building physical tools to probe biological molecules, using nanofabrication, lasers, microfluidics, electronics and biochemistry to generate data.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www2.lsdiv.harvard.edu/labs/cohen/ |title=The Cohen Group |access-date=2011-05-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628111746/http://www2.lsdiv.harvard.edu/labs/cohen/ |archive-date=2011-06-28 |url-status=dead }}</ref> His current research includes single-molecule spectroscopy of microbial [[rhodopsin]]s, the motion of bacteria in mucus, and new magneto-optical and chiroptical effects in organic molecules.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://investing.businessweek.com/businessweek/research/stocks/private/person.asp?personId=84939138&privcapId=79322247&previousCapId=79322247&previousTitle=Ion+Torrent+Systems+Incorporated|website=investing.businessweek.com|title=Stocks|access-date=2018-10-24}}{{dead link|date=April 2023|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

===Inventions===
In fifth grade, Cohen invented an "alarm" clock that woke him by playing a prerecorded message. 
In high school, Cohen created an eye-tracking apparatus for neuroscience experiments to benefit the disabled, an electrochemical hard disk drive,<ref name="electrochemical1"/> and a device that applies physics to allow his eye movements to maneuver his computer cursor.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2009/4/28/adam-e-cohen-with-cropped-blond/|title=Adam E. Cohen|date=April 28, 2009|work=Fifteen Minutes|publisher=The Harvard Crimson|access-date=May 3, 2011|archive-date=October 6, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121006082905/http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2009/4/28/adam-e-cohen-with-cropped-blond/|url-status=live}}</ref> 
He also invented and built a nanoscale patterning technique using an electrochemical [[scanning tunneling microscope]] in his bedroom, which led to winning the [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref name="prnewswire1">{{Cite web |url=http://www2.prnewswire.com/cgi-bin/stories.pl?ACCT=104&STORY=%2Fwww%2Fstory%2F73980&EDATE |title=Student Inventor from New York City Wins $40,000 Scholarship In 56th Westinghouse Science Talent Search |access-date=2018-10-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120509230745/http://www2.prnewswire.com/cgi-bin/stories.pl?ACCT=104&STORY=%2Fwww%2Fstory%2F73980&EDATE |archive-date=2012-05-09 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/news/1997/03/11/1997-03-11_a_young_mister_wizard__westi.html|title=Young Mister Wizard Westinghouse Prize for Manhattan Teen|website=[[New York Daily News]] }}</ref> His success in the Westinghouse competition led the mayor of New York City, [[Rudy Giuliani]], to declare March 12, 1997 "Adam Ezra Cohen Day".<ref>{{cite news | url=http://articles.nydailynews.com/2008-04-06/local/29431521_1_sequencing-shivani-sud-top-high-school-science | location=New York | work=Daily News | title=Science champs are still big lab rats | date=April 6, 2008 | access-date=2011-05-15 | archive-date=2012-05-09 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120509212241/http://articles.nydailynews.com/2008-04-06/local/29431521_1_sequencing-shivani-sud-top-high-school-science | url-status=dead }}</ref>
For his dissertation at Stanford, Cohen invented the Anti-Brownian Electrokinetic trap, known as the ABEL trap, a machine capable of trapping and manipulating individual biomolecules in solution.{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

===Awards===
In high school, Cohen won the [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]], now the Regeneron Science Talent Search, for an invention that involved building a scanning tunneling microscope in his bedroom.<ref name="prnewswire1"/> 
He was also inducted into the National Gallery for America’s Young Inventors for the same invention in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nmoe.org/gallery/i98.htm|title=National Gallery for America's Young Inventors|website=www.nmoe.org|access-date=2018-10-10|archive-date=2018-10-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181018044904/http://www.nmoe.org/gallery/i98.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>
In 2007, he was named to the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] ''[[Technology Review]]'' [[TR35]] as one of the top 35 innovators in the world under the age of 35.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.technologyreview.com/tr35/?year=2007 |title=2007 Young Innovators Under 35 |publisher=[[Technology Review]] |year=2007 |access-date=August 15, 2011 |archive-date=August 6, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110806160907/http://www.technologyreview.com/tr35/?year=2007 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="auto"/>
In 2012, ''Popular Science'' named Cohen one of the "Brilliant 10: the 10 most promising young scientists working today". In 2010 he won a [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]] under the [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]].<ref name="whitehouse1"/> and a [[NIH Director's New Innovator Award]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://commonfund.nih.gov/newinnovator/recipients10.aspx|title=NIH Director's New Innovator Award Program |website=commonfund.nih.gov|access-date=2011-05-03|archive-date=2011-09-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110916060624/http://commonfund.nih.gov/newinnovator/Recipients10.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> 
In 2014, he won the inaugural national [[Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists|Blavatnik National Award for Young Scientists]], awarded by the Blavatnik Family Foundation and the [[New York Academy of Sciences]] to "celebrate America’s most innovative and promising faculty-rank scientists and engineers".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blavatnikawards.org/news/items/2014-national-laureates/|title=2014 National Laureates - Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists|website=blavatnikawards.org|access-date=2014-07-29|archive-date=2014-08-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140809103016/http://blavatnikawards.org/news/items/2014-national-laureates/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nyas.org/awards/blavatnikawards/main.aspx |title=Archived copy |access-date=2014-07-29 |archive-date=2014-07-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140723205443/https://www.nyas.org/Awards/BlavatnikAwards/Main.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref>
